chapter.title: Choosing who to watch and where to look

cards.body: Forty web pages a day will kill this agent by Friday. Not because the code breaks, but because you stop opening a note that runs to 40 lines. **Your clipping person reads 5 newspapers, not the whole newsstand**, and only the pages where rivals print real news: prices, release notes, job ads.
cards.simpler: If the agent checks 40 web pages a day, you will stop using it within a week. The code will keep working. The problem is the note it writes. It will run to 40 lines, and you will stop opening it. Think of a person who clips newspaper stories for you. **They read 5 newspapers, not every paper on the stand**, and only the pages where rivals print real news: prices, release notes, job ads.

cards.prompt: You sell meal-kit boxes in Leeds. Your rival GreenCrate has 30 pages on its site. Which one page do you hand the clipping person first?

options.text: The About Us page with the founders' story
The homepage banner with the photo of a smiling family

whyNot.a: That's the furniture, not the news: an About page changes maybe once a year, so the clipping stays empty.
whyNot.c: That's the shop window, not the price tag: banners swap photos every week, so you get change without meaning.

cards.reteach: The agent only earns its keep on pages that change in ways you care about. A pricing page changes rarely, and every change is a decision someone made. A banner changes often and tells you nothing.

cards.title: Who makes the list
cards.body:
Start with the rivals a buyer compares you against on the same afternoon. Not the giant you dream of beating. The 3 to 5 names that come up when a customer says 'we're also looking at'.

Michael Porter's *Competitive Strategy* lists 4 things worth knowing about a rival: what they want, what they're doing now, what they believe, and what they can do. You'd think the job is to know everything about them. It's to know those 4, and a page only helps if it moves one of them.

Write the names down. **5 is the ceiling, not the target.**
cards.simpler: Start with the rivals a buyer compares you with. Not the giant you dream of beating. The 3 to 5 names that come up when a customer says 'we're also looking at'. Michael Porter's *Competitive Strategy* names 4 things worth knowing about a rival: what they want, what they do now, what they believe, what they can do. A page only helps if it moves one of them. Write the names down. **5 is the ceiling, not the target.**

cards.title: Dana's list of 12
cards.body: Dana runs a 6-person bookkeeping app, and her first watch list had 12 competitors, including Intuit, whose site is enormous. Exactly 1 of its pages mattered to her: the plan comparison. She cut the list to 4 rivals, 2 her size, 1 a bit bigger, and that single Intuit page. **The first morning's note was 9 lines**, and she read every one. With the list of 12 it would have been about 70 lines, and she would not have.
cards.simpler: Dana runs a bookkeeping app with 6 people. Her first watch list had 12 competitors, including Intuit, whose website is huge. Only 1 Intuit page mattered: the one that compares its plans. She cut the list to 4 rivals, 2 her size, 1 a bit bigger, plus that single Intuit page. **The first morning's note was 9 lines**, and she read every one. With 12 rivals it would have been about 70 lines, and she would not have read it.

cards.prompt: Dana wants a second page for a rival called Ledgerly. Which pick follows the rule?

options.text: Ledgerly's changelog, which lists each new feature with a date
Ledgerly's Twitter feed, about 20 posts a day
Ledgerly's homepage, because it's the front door

whyNot.b: That's the newsstand, not the paper: 20 posts a day is volume, and most of it is replies and memes.
whyNot.c: That's the front door, not the notice board: homepages change their photos and slogans, rarely their facts.

cards.reteach: Ask of each page: when it changes, is that a decision someone made? A changelog entry is a decision. A new homepage photo is a Tuesday.

cards.title: Which pages make the list
cards.body:
For each name, pick 1 or 2 pages where **a change means a decision**. Four kinds usually qualify: *pricing* (what they charge), *changelog* or release notes (what they built), *blog* (what they want you to think), and *careers* (what they're about to build; a job ad for a Head of Payments is a 6-month head start on a payments feature).

Then open each page and copy its exact web address, not the site name. Tomorrow's agent needs the same door, not the building.

That's the list. 3 to 5 names, 5 to 10 addresses, a one-line reason for each.
cards.simpler: Pick 1 or 2 pages per name where **a change means a decision**. Four kinds count: pricing (what they charge), changelog or release notes (what they built), blog (what they want you to think), careers (what they're about to build). A job ad for a Head of Payments means a payments feature in 6 months. Copy each page's exact web address, not just the site name. End with 3 to 5 names, 5 to 10 addresses, a reason for each.

cards.body: Tom added every rival's blog, press page, help centre, status page and LinkedIn. By Thursday the note ran to 3 screens and he stopped opening it, and nobody noticed, least of all the agent. The sign to spot: **you skim the note instead of reading it**. When that happens, cut pages until you read every line again.
cards.simpler: Tom added every rival's blog, press page, help centre, status page and LinkedIn. By Thursday the note filled 3 screens. He stopped opening it, and nobody noticed, least of all the agent. The warning sign is this: **you skim the note instead of reading it**. When that happens, cut pages until you read every line again.

cards.prompt: A friend shows you their watch list: 8 competitors, 6 pages each, 48 addresses. What do you fix first?

options.text: Add the exact web addresses, since site names aren't enough
Cut it to 3 to 5 competitors with 1 or 2 pages each that change for a reason
Swap the 6 pages per rival for their social feeds, which update more often

whyNot.a: That's chapter 3's problem, not today's: exact addresses matter, but 48 right addresses is still 48 pages nobody reads.
whyNot.c: That's more noise, not less: the problem is change without meaning, and a social feed is the purest form of it.

cards.reteach: The list is a diet, not a buffet. Fewer pages means a note you actually read, and a note you read is the only kind that changes what you do tomorrow.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Pick the 3 to 5 rivals a buyer compares you with, and for each pick 1 or 2 pages where a change means someone made a decision: pricing, changelog, blog, careers. Write down the exact addresses and why each is worth reading, because **a short note you read beats a long one you skim**.

Tomorrow: a web page is just text. Mostly. The exceptions teach you the most.
cards.simpler: Pick the 3 to 5 rivals a buyer compares you with. For each one, pick 1 or 2 pages where a change means someone made a decision: pricing, changelog, blog, careers. Write down the exact web addresses and why each one is worth reading. The rule behind all of it: **a short note you read beats a long one you skim**. Tomorrow's topic: a web page is just text. Mostly. The exceptions teach you the most.

cards.body: Open your notes app. Write 3 rival names. Under each, paste 1 exact web address and finish this sentence: 'I want to know the day this changes because...'
cards.simpler: Open your notes app. Write down 3 rival names. Under each name, paste 1 exact web address, the full link to the page, not just the company's site. Then finish this sentence for each: **'I want to know the day this changes because...'** That sentence is your one-line reason for watching the page.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now write a watch list of 3 to 5 competitors with 1 or 2 exact web addresses each, and say why every page is worth reading.
